key_terms.meaning: Each switch on for 180°; output ±V<sub>dc</sub> (full bridge) with fundamental peak 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π
Anti-parallel diode that returns inductive load current to the bus just after switching
Three switches on; phase steps V<sub>dc</sub>/3, 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3; V<sub>L</sub> = 0.816V<sub>dc</sub>
Two switches on; phase ±V<sub>dc</sub>/2 with 60° gaps; V<sub>L</sub> = 0.707V<sub>dc</sub>
One pulse 2d wide per half cycle: V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>√(2d/π), b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nd
p equal pulses per half cycle; strongest harmonics at 2p ± 1
m<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>r</sub>/V<sub>c</sub> sets the voltage; m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>m</sub> sets the harmonic positions
Fundamental m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>; first harmonics at m<sub>f</sub> (bipolar) or 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1 (unipolar)
V<sub>L1</sub> = 0.612 m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub>; third-harmonic injection allows m<sub>a</sub> = 1.155
Active vectors 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 long; T<sub>x</sub> = mT<sub>s</sub> sin(60° − θ), T<sub>y</sub> = mT<sub>s</sub> sin θ
N angles per quarter: fundamental plus N − 1 harmonics set by the angles
Stiff link current I<sub>d</sub>; line current 120° quasi-square, I<sub>1</sub> = 0.78I<sub>d</sub>
s cells per phase give 2s + 1 levels, peak sV<sub>cell</sub>
i* = I* sin(θ + φ*), θ from the PLL

takeaways: A square-wave bridge fixes the output by the bus: 0.9V<sub>dc</sub> fundamental rms for the full bridge, with odd harmonics of 1/n.
With an R-L load the voltage stays square, the current is exponential, and the feedback diodes conduct after every switching.
In 180° mode three switches conduct and the phase voltage is a six-step wave; in 120° mode two conduct and the output is lower.
Single and multiple pulse modulation vary the fundamental by pulse width; more pulses move the harmonics up to 2p ± 1.
Sinusoidal PWM makes the fundamental m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> and pushes the harmonics to the carrier; unipolar SPWM doubles their frequency.
Space vector modulation averages two active vectors and the zero vectors each period and reaches 15.5 % more voltage than SPWM.
Harmonic elimination solves for switching angles that zero chosen harmonics; N angles remove N − 1 of them.
A CSI holds the link current, needs reverse-blocking switches and overlap, survives shorts and regenerates easily.
Multilevel inverters divide the bus into steps, lowering device voltage, dv/dt and THD at the cost of more parts and balancing.
A grid-tied inverter is a controlled current source: the PLL gives the angle, the outer loop the amplitude, the inner loop the waveform.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to carry the circuit, a switching table or sequence, the waveforms with their levels marked, and one worked set of numbers. Most syllabi ask for the 180° and 120° modes with phase and line waveforms, the single-pulse, multiple-pulse and sinusoidal PWM methods with their harmonic spectra, and the current source inverter.

bank.q: Draw a single-phase full-bridge inverter feeding an R-L load. Explain its four modes of operation over one cycle with the load voltage and current waveforms, and derive the Fourier series of the output voltage.
outline: Bridge of four switches with anti-parallel diodes; load between leg midpoints
S1, S4 and S2, S3 gated alternately for 180°
Four modes: D1 D4, S1 S4, D2 D3, S2 S3
Square voltage, exponential current, I<sub>max</sub> formula
answer: Circuit: a DC source V<sub>dc</sub> feeds two legs, S1 over S2 and S3 over S4. Each switch has an anti-parallel diode D1 to D4. The R-L load is connected between the leg midpoints A and B.
Gating: S1 and S4 are gated from 0 to T/2 and S2 and S3 from T/2 to T. So v<sub>AB</sub> = +V<sub>dc</sub> in the first half period and −V<sub>dc</sub> in the second, whatever the current does.

answer.text: Modes over one cycle (current i taken positive from A to B):

answer: Waveforms: v<sub>AB</sub> is a ±V<sub>dc</sub> square wave. The current rises exponentially towards +V<sub>dc</sub>/R with time constant τ = L/R in the positive half and falls towards −V<sub>dc</sub>/R in the negative half, swinging between −I<sub>max</sub> and +I<sub>max</sub>. The diodes conduct just after each switching, until the current passes zero; this is why they are called feedback diodes.

Steady state: starting the half period at −I<sub>max</sub>, i(t) = V<sub>dc</sub>/R − (V<sub>dc</sub>/R + I<sub>max</sub>) e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. Setting i(T/2) = +I<sub>max</sub> gives I<sub>max</sub> = (V<sub>dc</sub>/R) tanh(T/4τ), and i = 0 at t<sub>x</sub> = τ ln(1 + tanh(T/4τ)).

answer.text: Fourier series: the wave is odd and has half-wave symmetry, so only odd sine terms remain:
answer.pre:
b<sub>n</sub> = (2/π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> V<sub>dc</sub> sin nθ dθ × 2/2 = (2V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ)(1 − cos nπ)
    = 4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ for odd n, 0 for even n
v<sub>AB</sub> = Σ<sub>n = 1, 3, 5, …</sub> (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nωt

answer: Harmonic current: i = Σ (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ|Z<sub>n</sub>|) sin(nωt − φ<sub>n</sub>), with |Z<sub>n</sub>| = √(R² + (nωL)²) and φ<sub>n</sub> = tan⁻¹(nωL/R). The fundamental rms voltage is 0.9V<sub>dc</sub>.

Check with numbers: V<sub>dc</sub> = 220 V, R = 10 Ω, L = 25 mH, 50 Hz give τ = 2.5 ms, I<sub>max</sub> = 22 × tanh 2 = 21.21 A and t<sub>x</sub> = 1.69 ms, so the diodes conduct for 1.69 ms of each 10 ms half period.

answer.text: Harmonic currents for the same numbers (ωL = 7.854 Ω): the impedance grows with n, so the current harmonics fall much faster than the voltage harmonics.

answer: The rms current is √(15.577² + 2.579² + 0.978² + 0.506²) = 15.83 A, so the load takes 15.83² × 10 = 2507 W and the supply gives an average current of 2507/220 = 11.40 A. The fundamental current lags its voltage by 38.1°, which is why part of each half cycle is spent in the diodes.

bank.q: Compare 180° and 120° conduction of a three-phase bridge inverter feeding a balanced star resistive load. Give the switching sequence, the phase and line voltage waveforms and their rms values.
outline: Switch numbering and gating order every 60°
180°: three switches on, phase steps V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, line quasi-square
120°: two switches on, phase ±V<sub>dc</sub>/2 with gaps, line four-level
answer: Bridge: leg A has S1 (top) and S4, leg B S3 and S6, leg C S5 and S2, so a new switch is gated every 60° in the order S1 to S6.
180° mode: each switch is gated for 180°, so three switches (one per leg) are on in each 60° interval: S5 S6 S1, S6 S1 S2, S1 S2 S3, S2 S3 S4, S3 S4 S5, S4 S5 S6.

Equivalent circuit for 0° to 60°: A and C are on the positive rail and B on the negative. The A and C phases are in parallel (R/2) and in series with B (R), so i = V<sub>dc</sub>/(1.5R), v<sub>AN</sub> = v<sub>CN</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and v<sub>BN</sub> = −2V<sub>dc</sub>/3. Repeating for each interval gives the six-step phase voltage V<sub>dc</sub>/3, 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3.

Line voltage in 180° mode: v<sub>AB</sub> = v<sub>AN</sub> − v<sub>BN</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub> from 0° to 120°, 0 from 120° to 180°, −V<sub>dc</sub> from 180° to 300°, 0 from 300° to 360°: a 120° quasi-square.

120° mode: each switch is gated for 120°, two switches are on at a time (S6 S1, S1 S2, S2 S3, S3 S4, S4 S5, S5 S6), and the third terminal floats. With a resistive load the two connected phases each take V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and the floating one 0, so v<sub>AN</sub> = +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 for 120°, 0 for 60°, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 for 120°, 0 for 60°. The line voltage steps through V<sub>dc</sub>, V<sub>dc</sub>/2, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2, −V<sub>dc</sub>, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2, V<sub>dc</sub>/2.

answer.text: rms values:

head: Quantity
180° mode
120° mode
rows: Gap between top and bottom switch

answer: Comparison: 180° mode uses the switches better and gives a higher output; 120° mode has a natural 60° gap that makes shoot-through unlikely, but its floating phase lets an inductive load distort the voltage. Both waveforms have no triplen harmonics; the lowest are the 5th and 7th.

answer.text: Fourier series of the 180° line voltage, a 120° quasi-square:
answer.pre:
v<sub>AB</sub> = Σ (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) cos(nπ/6) sin n(ωt + π/6),  n = 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, …
V<sub>L1</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π)(√3/2)/√2 = (√6/π)V<sub>dc</sub> = 0.780V<sub>dc</sub>

answer: 120° equivalent circuit: in each 60° interval only two phases are in series across the bus (2R), so the current is V<sub>dc</sub>/2R and each connected phase takes V<sub>dc</sub>/2; the third phase carries nothing. The phase voltage therefore has the 120° quasi-square shape and the line voltage the four-level shape.
Check: for V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V, 180° mode gives V<sub>L</sub> = 326.6 V and V<sub>P</sub> = 188.6 V; 120° mode gives V<sub>L</sub> = 282.8 V and V<sub>P</sub> = 163.3 V.

bank.q: Explain single-pulse, multiple-pulse and sinusoidal pulse-width modulation for voltage control of a single-phase inverter. Compare their harmonic content.
outline: Why voltage control: fixed V<sub>dc</sub>, variable output
Single pulse: reference square vs carrier, width 2d, V<sub>rms</sub> and b<sub>n</sub>
Multiple pulse: p pulses per half cycle, harmonics at 2p ± 1
Sinusoidal: sine vs triangle, m<sub>a</sub> and m<sub>f</sub>, harmonics near m<sub>f</sub>
answer: Need: a motor, a UPS or a heater needs a variable fundamental from a fixed bus. The full bridge can apply +V<sub>dc</sub>, −V<sub>dc</sub> or 0, so the output is controlled by the width and position of pulses within each half cycle.

Single-pulse modulation: a rectangular reference of amplitude A<sub>r</sub> is compared with a triangular carrier at twice the output frequency, giving one pulse of width 2d = (A<sub>r</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>) × 180° centred in each half cycle. V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>√(2d/π) and b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nd. The 3rd harmonic is large; it vanishes only for 2d = 120°.

Multiple-pulse (symmetric) modulation: the carrier is raised to 2pf, giving p equal pulses of width 2d per half cycle. V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>√(2pd/π) and b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nd Σ sin nγ<sub>k</sub> over the pulse centres γ<sub>k</sub>. The strongest harmonics move to 2p ± 1; the price is 4p switching edges per cycle.

Sinusoidal PWM: a sine reference V<sub>r</sub> sin ωt is compared with a triangle of peak V<sub>c</sub> at f<sub>c</sub>. The pulse widths follow a sine, so the fundamental is m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> (m<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>r</sub>/V<sub>c</sub> ≤ 1) and the harmonics sit at m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>/f and its sidebands (bipolar) or at 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1 (unipolar).

answer.text: Comparison for a full bridge:

answer: Example: on a 200 V bus, a 60° single pulse gives 127.3 V fundamental peak with a 3rd harmonic of 84.9 V (67 %); four 10° pulses give 94.3 V rms with the 7th and 9th strongest; SPWM with m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8 gives 160 V peak with no harmonic below the carrier sidebands.

Generation in practice: the single-pulse and multiple-pulse gate signals come from one comparator fed with a rectangular reference; sinusoidal PWM uses the same comparator with a sine reference. In all three, the comparator output drives S1, S4 and its complement S2, S3 through dead-time logic.

Distortion at low output: for single-pulse control at small d, every harmonic b<sub>n</sub> ≈ (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π)d is as large as the fundamental, so the THD rises steeply as the output is reduced. Multiple pulses spread the same on-time over the half cycle and lower the 3rd, 5th and 7th; sinusoidal widths go further and leave almost nothing below m<sub>f</sub> − 2.

Conclusion: all three keep V<sub>dc</sub> fixed. Moving from one pulse to many and then to sinusoidal widths moves the distortion upward in frequency, where the load inductance or a small filter removes it, at the cost of more switching.

bank.q: Explain the working of a single-phase capacitor-commutated current source inverter with a resistive load, derive its circuit turn-off time, and compare a CSI with a VSI.
outline: Circuit: L<sub>d</sub>, four thyristors, C across the load
t<sub>c</sub> = RC ln(1 + tanh(T/4RC)) → RC ln 2
answer: Circuit: a DC source with a large series inductor L<sub>d</sub> supplies a constant current I<sub>d</sub> to a bridge of thyristors T1, T2 (one diagonal) and T3, T4 (the other). The load R has a capacitor C across it.

Operation: with T1, T2 on, +I<sub>d</sub> flows into the R-C pair; with T3, T4 on, −I<sub>d</sub>. The load current pair is therefore a ±I<sub>d</sub> square wave, and the capacitor voltage v rises exponentially towards ±I<sub>d</sub> R.

answer.text: Derivation, for one half period starting just after T1, T2 are fired (v = −V<sub>0</sub>):
answer.pre:
C dv/dt + v/R = I<sub>d</sub>
v(t) = I<sub>d</sub>R − (I<sub>d</sub>R + V<sub>0</sub>) e<sup>−t/RC</sup>
v(T/2) = +V<sub>0</sub>  ⇒  V<sub>0</sub> = I<sub>d</sub>R tanh(T/4RC)

answer: Commutation: when T3, T4 are fired, the capacitor voltage +V<sub>0</sub> appears in reverse across T1 and T2. Their current drops to zero at once and they stay reverse-biased while v swings from −V<sub>0</sub> (seen from the new conduction path) to zero.

answer.text: Turn-off time:
answer.pre:
0 = I<sub>d</sub>R − (I<sub>d</sub>R + V<sub>0</sub>) e<sup>−t<sub>c</sub>/RC</sup>
t<sub>c</sub> = RC ln(1 + V<sub>0</sub>/I<sub>d</sub>R) = RC ln(1 + tanh(T/4RC))
for T/2 ≫ RC: t<sub>c</sub> = RC ln 2 = 0.693RC

answer: Numbers: I<sub>d</sub> = 20 A, R = 10 Ω, C = 20 μF, 500 Hz give RC = 200 μs, T/4RC = 2.50, V<sub>0</sub> = 197.3 V and t<sub>c</sub> = 137.3 μs, enough for thyristors with t<sub>q</sub> = 40 μs.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Role of L<sub>d</sub> and overlap: L<sub>d</sub> must be large enough that I<sub>d</sub> stays nearly constant over a half period. The incoming pair is fired before the outgoing pair stops, so the current always has a path; firing both pairs at once only shorts the load side for a moment, which a CSI tolerates.

Three-phase form: in the auto-sequential commutated inverter (ASCI), six thyristors conduct for 120° each; delta-connected commutating capacitors in each group and series diodes that isolate the capacitors from the load give the same capacitor commutation for each phase in turn. The line current is the 120° quasi-square of height I<sub>d</sub>, with fundamental 0.78I<sub>d</sub>.
Conclusion: the CSI is rugged against shorts and regenerates easily, which suits high-power drives and induction heating; the VSI is simpler, smaller and faster, which suits general use.

bank.q: A single-phase full-bridge inverter has a resistive load R = 2.4 Ω and a DC input of 48 V, in square-wave mode. Find (a) the rms fundamental output voltage, (b) the output power, (c) the average and peak current of each switch, (d) the peak blocking voltage of each switch, (e) the THD, (f) the distortion factor, and (g) the harmonic factor and distortion factor of the lowest-order harmonic.
outline: Switch current V<sub>dc</sub>/R peak, half of it average
answer: The output is a ±48 V square wave, so V<sub>o</sub>(rms) = 48 V.
(b) P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R = 48²/2.4 = 960 W. The fundamental alone gives 43.22²/2.4 = 778.1 W.
(c) Peak load current = 48/2.4 = 20 A. Each switch conducts for half the period, so its average current is 10 A and its peak 20 A.
(d) An off switch is across the whole bus: peak blocking voltage = 48 V.

answer.text: (f) Distortion factor: each harmonic is weighted by 1/n², as a second-order filter would weight it.

answer: (g) The lowest-order harmonic is the 3rd: V<sub>3</sub> = V<sub>1</sub>/3, so HF<sub>3</sub> = V<sub>3</sub>/V<sub>1</sub> = 33.33 % and DF<sub>3</sub> = (V<sub>3</sub>/3²)/V<sub>1</sub> = 1/27 = 3.70 %.
Method: the square wave of height V<sub>dc</sub> has V<sub>n</sub> = 4V<sub>dc</sub>/(nπ√2) for odd n, so every figure of merit can be written in V<sub>1</sub> alone: V<sub>n</sub> = V<sub>1</sub>/n.

answer.text: The lowest harmonics:

answer: Switch duty: each switch conducts for 10 ms of every 20 ms and carries 20 A, so it dissipates its conduction loss at 10 A average; the DC supply delivers 20 A, the same as the load power divided by V<sub>dc</sub> (960/48).
Why the DF is so much smaller than the THD: the 1/n² weighting models a second-order filter. Most of the 48 % THD sits in the 3rd, 5th and 7th, which such a filter attenuates by 9, 25 and 49 times.
Check: V<sub>1</sub>² + Σ V<sub>n</sub>² must equal V<sub>o</sub>²; with THD 48.34 %, V<sub>1</sub>√(1 + THD²) = 43.22 × 1.1107 = 48.00 V = V<sub>o</sub>.

bank.q: A three-phase bridge inverter feeds a star-connected resistive load of 10 Ω per phase from a 450 V DC source. For 180° and for 120° conduction find (a) the rms phase and line voltages, (b) the rms load current, (c) the rms and peak switch current and (d) the load power.
outline: Phase voltage steps in each mode
rms by squaring over the cycle
Switch current = phase current for half (180°) or one third (120°) of the cycle
answer: 180° mode: the phase voltage is 150 V for 120° and 300 V for 60° in each half cycle, so V<sub>P</sub> = √[(2 × 150² + 300²)/3] = (√2/3)V<sub>dc</sub> = 212.1 V and V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>P</sub> = 367.4 V.
I<sub>P</sub> = 212.1/10 = 21.21 A; the peak, in the single phase of each interval, is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3R = 30 A.
Each top switch carries its phase current for the positive half cycle: I<sub>sw</sub> = I<sub>P</sub>/√2 = 15.00 A rms, 30 A peak.

120° mode: each phase is at ±225 V for 120° per half cycle and 0 for 60°. V<sub>P</sub> = 225√(2/3) = 183.7 V; the line voltage is 450 V for 60° and 225 V for 120° per half cycle: V<sub>L</sub> = √[(450² + 2 × 225²)/3] = 318.2 V.
I<sub>P</sub> = 183.7/10 = 18.37 A. Each switch carries V<sub>dc</sub>/2R = 22.5 A for 120°: I<sub>sw</sub> = 22.5/√3 = 12.99 A rms.

answer.text: Summary:
Phase voltage v<sub>AN</sub> over one cycle (in volts):

answer: Fundamental phase voltages: 180° mode (√2/π)V<sub>dc</sub> = 99.0 V; 120° mode (4/π)(V<sub>dc</sub>/2)cos 30°/√2 = 85.8 V. The 120° mode gives about 13 % less fundamental from the same bus.

Interpretation: in 180° mode each phase is always connected, so the load sees power for the whole cycle; in 120° mode each phase is disconnected for a third of the cycle, which is why both the voltage and the power are lower.

bank.q: A single-phase full bridge on a 220 V bus uses symmetric multiple-pulse modulation with four pulses per half cycle. Find the pulse width that makes the fundamental 60 % of the square-wave value, the rms output and the main harmonics. What carrier frequency is needed for a 50 Hz output?
outline: b<sub>1</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π) sin d Σ sin γ<sub>k</sub>
answer: With p = 4 pulses per half cycle, each pulse can be at most 45° wide and the pulse centres are γ<sub>k</sub> = (k − ½) × 45° = 22.5°, 67.5°, 112.5° and 157.5°.

answer.text: Fundamental of p pulses of width 2d:
answer.pre:
b<sub>1</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π) sin d Σ sin γ<sub>k</sub>
Σ sin γ<sub>k</sub> = 2(sin 22.5° + sin 67.5°) = 2(0.3827 + 0.9239) = 2.6131

answer: Setting b<sub>1</sub> = 0.6 × 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π gives sin d = 0.6/2.6131 = 0.2296, so d = 13.27° and each pulse is 2d = 26.55° wide.
Total on-time per half cycle = 4 × 26.55° = 106.2°, so V<sub>rms</sub> = 220√(106.2/180) = 169.0 V. The fundamental is 0.6 × 4 × 220/π = 168.1 V peak (118.8 V rms).

answer.text: Harmonics from b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nd Σ sin nγ<sub>k</sub>:

answer: The strongest harmonics are the 7th and 9th (2p ∓ 1), as expected; the 3rd and 5th remain at 39 % and 33 %.
Carrier: p = f<sub>c</sub>/2f, so f<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 4 × 50 = 400 Hz, and the modulation index is M = 2d/45° = 0.590.

answer.text: Derivation of the multiple-pulse coefficient (half-wave symmetry, odd n):
answer.pre:
b<sub>n</sub> = (2/π) Σ<sub>k</sub> ∫<sub>γk−d</sub><sup>γk+d</sup> V<sub>dc</sub> sin nθ dθ
    = (2V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) Σ<sub>k</sub> [cos n(γ<sub>k</sub> − d) − cos n(γ<sub>k</sub> + d)]
    = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ) sin nd Σ<sub>k</sub> sin nγ<sub>k</sub>

answer: Comparison with one pulse: a single pulse giving the same fundamental (sin d = 0.6) would be 73.7° wide and have a 3rd harmonic of 52 % of the fundamental, against 39 % here, so the four-pulse pattern trades a cleaner low-order spectrum for 16 switching edges per cycle instead of 4.

bank.q: A single-phase full-bridge inverter uses unipolar SPWM with V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V, m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8, a 10 kHz carrier and a 50 Hz output. Find the fundamental output, the frequency ratio, the frequencies and sizes of the first harmonic group, and compare with bipolar SPWM at the same carrier.
answer: Fundamental: V<sub>1,peak</sub> = m<sub>a</sub> V<sub>dc</sub> = 0.8 × 400 = 320 V, so V<sub>1</sub> = 226.3 V rms.
Frequency ratio: m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>m</sub> = 10000/50 = 200.

Unipolar: the legs compare +v<sub>r</sub> and −v<sub>r</sub> with one carrier, so the harmonics at m<sub>f</sub> and its sidebands cancel between the legs. The first group is at 2m<sub>f</sub> ± 1 = 399 and 401, i.e. 19.95 kHz and 20.05 kHz, each 0.314V<sub>dc</sub> = 126 V peak at m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8.
Bipolar at the same carrier: the largest harmonic is at m<sub>f</sub>, 10 kHz, of 0.818V<sub>dc</sub> = 327 V peak, with sidebands at 9.9 and 10.1 kHz of 0.220V<sub>dc</sub> = 88 V.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Filter: an L-C filter falls at 40 dB per decade above its corner; the unipolar ripple is twice as far up and smaller, so for the same output ripple the filter can be about four times smaller in LC product.

answer.text: Switch states of unipolar SPWM (leg A compares +v<sub>r</sub>, leg B compares −v<sub>r</sub>):

answer: Why the m<sub>f</sub> group cancels: leg B sees the same carrier and an inverted reference, so its carrier harmonic is identical to that of leg A and disappears in v<sub>o</sub> = v<sub>AO</sub> − v<sub>BO</sub>, while the fundamentals add. The remaining output pulses occur twice per carrier period, so the ripple is centred on 2f<sub>c</sub>.

Conclusion: unipolar SPWM halves the voltage steps and doubles the ripple frequency with the same switching loss, which is why most single-phase inverters use it; bipolar SPWM needs only one comparator and has no common-mode jump at the load terminals.

bank.q: A three-phase VSI on a 600 V bus must give 400 V rms line to line at 50 Hz, switching at 5 kHz. Show that sine-triangle PWM cannot give this in its linear range but space vector modulation can. For a reference at 75°, find the sector, the dwell times, the seven-segment sequence and the leg on-times.
outline: Sequence with one leg change per step and leg times
answer: Limits: SPWM gives at most 0.6124 × 600 = 367.4 V rms line to line, less than 400 V, so it would have to overmodulate. SVM gives up to V<sub>dc</sub>/√2 = 424.3 V, so 400 V is inside its linear range.
Reference: phase peak V<sub>m</sub> = 400√2/√3 = 326.6 V; m = √3 × 326.6/600 = 0.9428 (less than 1). T<sub>s</sub> = 1/5000 = 200 μs.
Sector: α = 75° lies between 60° and 120°, so sector 2, bounded by V<sub>x</sub> = V2 (110) and V<sub>y</sub> = V3 (010); θ = 75° − 60° = 15°.

answer.text: Dwell times:

answer: Sequence: to change one leg per step, go 000 → 010 → 110 → 111 → 110 → 010 → 000, i.e. V0 (T<sub>0</sub>/4 = 4.47 μs), V3 (T<sub>y</sub>/2 = 24.4 μs), V2 (T<sub>x</sub>/2 = 66.7 μs), V7 (T<sub>0</sub>/2 = 8.93 μs), then back in reverse order.

answer.text: Leg on-times (bit = 1):

head: Leg
States in which it is on
On-time per period (μs)
Duty

answer: Why it works: in sector 2 phase b is the most positive and c the most negative, so b has the longest on-time and c the shortest, as the table shows. Adding the common-mode term −(max + min)/2 to the sine references gives the same duties.

Why SVM reaches further: the largest circle inside the hexagon has radius (2V<sub>dc</sub>/3) cos 30° = V<sub>dc</sub>/√3, a phase peak 15.5 % above the V<sub>dc</sub>/2 of sine-triangle PWM. In line rms this is V<sub>dc</sub>/√2 against 0.612V<sub>dc</sub>.

Check of V2 with the Clarke transform: state 110 gives phase voltages V<sub>dc</sub>/3, V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −2V<sub>dc</sub>/3; then v<sub>α</sub> = (2/3)(1/3 − 1/6 + 1/3)V<sub>dc</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and v<sub>β</sub> = (1/3 + 2/3)V<sub>dc</sub>/√3 = V<sub>dc</sub>/√3, a vector of length 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 at 60°, as drawn.

Implementation: the three on-times are loaded into the compare registers of a centre-aligned timer once per 200 μs period; the timer produces the symmetric seven-segment pattern by itself, with dead time added by the gate-drive logic.
Check: T<sub>x</sub> + T<sub>y</sub> = 182.1 μs = m T<sub>s</sub> cos(30° − θ) = 0.9428 × 200 × cos 15° = 182.1 μs, and T<sub>0</sub> > 0, so the point is inside the hexagon.

bank.q: Explain selective harmonic elimination. For a two-level square wave with two notches per quarter cycle, derive the condition for removing the 3rd and 5th harmonics, verify the angles 23.64° and 33.33°, and discuss what happens to the other harmonics.
outline: Quarter-wave symmetry: only odd sine terms
Energy moves to the 7th, 9th, 11th; other methods; three-phase triplens
answer: Idea: the harmonics of an inverter output are Fourier coefficients that depend on the switching angles. Choosing the angles so that chosen coefficients are zero removes those harmonics without a filter. With N free angles one equation sets the fundamental (or here, the fundamental is accepted as it comes) and the rest remove harmonics.
Symmetry: a wave that is odd and quarter-wave symmetric has only odd sine terms, b<sub>n</sub> = (4/π)∫_0<sup>π/2</sup> v sin nθ dθ.

answer.text: Two notches per quarter (v = +V<sub>dc</sub> on 0–α<sub>1</sub>, −V<sub>dc</sub> on α<sub>1</sub>–α<sub>2</sub>, +V<sub>dc</sub> on α<sub>2</sub>–90°):
answer.pre:
b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ)[(1 − cos nα<sub>1</sub>) − (cos nα<sub>1</sub> − cos nα<sub>2</sub>) + cos nα<sub>2</sub>]
    = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ)(1 − 2 cos nα<sub>1</sub> + 2 cos nα<sub>2</sub>)

answer: Conditions: 1 − 2 cos 3α<sub>1</sub> + 2 cos 3α<sub>2</sub> = 0 and 1 − 2 cos 5α<sub>1</sub> + 2 cos 5α<sub>2</sub> = 0. They are solved by Newton's method; a start at 20° and 30° converges to α<sub>1</sub> = 23.64°, α<sub>2</sub> = 33.33°.

answer.text: Verification:

head: n
1 − 2cos nα<sub>1</sub> + 2cos nα<sub>2</sub>
b<sub>n</sub> peak on a 220 V bus (V)

answer: The fundamental is 0.8389 × 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π = 84 % of the square-wave value, so little voltage is lost.

The other harmonics: the volt-seconds removed from the 3rd and 5th reappear at the 7th, 9th and 11th, which are now larger than in a plain square wave (where they would be 14 %, 11 % and 9 %). They are easier to filter because their frequency, and the reactance of the load, is higher.

Solving the equations: Newton's method starts from a guess (20°, 30°), evaluates the two residuals and their derivatives, and corrects both angles together; four or five iterations reach four decimals. A table of such solutions over the wanted range of output is stored in the controller.

Other ways to remove low harmonics: a 120° pulse removes the 3rd; two phase-shifted square-wave bridges added by transformers remove the nth when cos(nφ/2) = 0; a twelve-step arrangement removes the 5th and 7th; stepped (multilevel) waves remove harmonics by their step angles.

Three-phase: the triplen harmonics cancel in the line voltage, so the angles are spent on the 5th, 7th, 11th and 13th instead. Evaluation: SHE gives a clean low-order spectrum at a low switching frequency, ideal for large drives, but the angles must be stored for every output level and a change of output means a jump in the table.

bank.q: A single-phase grid-tied inverter must inject 5 kW at unity power factor into a 230 V grid. Explain how the PLL, the current controller and the DC-link voltage loop work together, and analyse what happens if the PLL angle is 5° in error.
outline: Grid is a voltage source; inverter is a current source
PLL gives θ; reference i* = I* sin(θ + φ*)
Inner current loop with PWM; outer DC-link loop sets I*
5° error: P and Q, and correction by the loops
answer: Principle: the grid fixes the voltage, so the inverter controls the current it injects. The voltage it must make is the grid voltage plus the drop across its filter, and this is produced automatically by the current loop.

PLL: measures the grid voltage and produces its angle θ and frequency; in a single-phase unit it compares the grid voltage with an internal sine and adjusts the internal frequency until the error is zero.

Current reference: i* = I* sin(θ + φ*), with φ* = 0 for unity power factor. The inner controller (PI in dq, PR in the stationary frame, or hysteresis) compares the measured current with i* and sets the PWM duty of the bridge each switching period; its bandwidth is about 1–2 kHz.

DC-link loop: if the PV array delivers more power than the inverter injects, the DC-link capacitor charges and its voltage rises. The slow outer loop (10–20 Hz) raises I* until the link voltage returns to its set point, so power in equals power out. The MPPT sets that set point.
Numbers: I = P/V = 5000/230 = 21.74 A rms, I* = 30.74 A peak.

answer.text: PLL error of 5°: the current leads (or lags) the voltage by 5°.

answer: Effect: the real power falls by 19 W, so the DC-link voltage rises and the outer loop raises I* by 1/cos 5° = 1.0038, to 21.82 A; the power is restored but the inverter now also exchanges about 437 var and runs at power factor 0.996. A large or changing error (weak grid, distorted voltage) can make the current loop interact with the grid impedance and become unstable.

Choice of PLL: a single-phase PLL builds a second, 90° shifted signal (a second-order generalised integrator or a transport delay) so that it can work like a three-phase dq PLL; its bandwidth is kept to a few tens of hertz so that grid harmonics do not disturb θ.

Harmonic limits: the current loop must also keep low-order current harmonics within the grid code, typically a few per cent THD; the PR controller can be given extra resonant terms at the 3rd, 5th and 7th for this.

Evaluation: the PLL sets the quality of the power factor, the current loop sets the waveform quality and harmonics, and the DC-link loop sets the power balance. A good design keeps the loops about a decade apart in bandwidth so that each sees the faster one as ideal.

bank.q: Evaluate a three-level neutral-point-clamped inverter against a two-level VSI for a 3.3 kV medium-voltage motor drive. Cover device voltage, harmonic content, dv/dt, component count and control complexity.
outline: DC bus from a 3.3 kV rectifier
Line voltage levels 3 against 5; dv/dt halves
answer: Bus: a six-pulse rectifier on 3.3 kV gives about 1.35 × 3300 = 4455 V DC.

Device voltage: in a two-level leg each switch blocks the whole bus, 4455 V, which needs the highest-voltage (and slowest) devices or devices in series. In a three-level NPC leg each switch blocks V<sub>dc</sub>/2 = 2228 V, within the range of standard high-voltage IGBTs.

Waveform: the two-level pole voltage has 2 levels and the line voltage 3; the NPC pole has 3 levels and the line 5. Each step is 2228 V instead of 4455 V, so dv/dt is halved for the same switching speed, which protects motor insulation and bearings and reduces reflected-wave overvoltage on long cables.

Harmonics: for the same switching frequency the three-level line voltage has roughly half the ripple, so the motor current THD and the torque ripple are lower, or the switching frequency can be lowered for the same THD.

answer.text: Components per inverter:

answer: Control: the NPC needs a midpoint-voltage balancing loop (by choosing between redundant small vectors) and more complex modulation; the two-level bridge needs only standard SPWM or SVM.

Losses: the NPC switches half the voltage, so switching loss per device falls, but current passes through two devices in series, so conduction loss rises; the inner switches carry more loss than the outer ones.

Effect on the motor: the five-level line voltage of the NPC follows the sine more closely; with the same 1 kHz switching the current ripple and the torque ripple are about halved, and the motor can often be used without the sine filter a two-level drive would need on a long cable.
Reliability: more parts mean more possible failures, but each device is less stressed; NPC drives can also run on with reduced output after some device failures, using the remaining redundant states.

Verdict: at 3.3 kV the NPC is preferred: it uses standard devices without series connection, halves dv/dt and improves the waveform, for twice the switches and a balancing loop. Below about 690 V the two-level bridge is cheaper and is the normal choice.

bank.q: Choose between a voltage source inverter and a current source inverter for a 5 MW pump drive that must survive output short circuits and return braking energy to the supply. Justify the choice.
outline: Link element and what it holds
Fault behaviour: short against open circuit
Commutation: LCI with a synchronous motor
answer: A VSI holds the DC voltage with a capacitor; its output voltage is set by the switches and the load sets the current. A CSI holds the DC current with an inductor; its output current is set by the switches and the load sets the voltage.

Short circuit: in a VSI the bus capacitor discharges straight into a short, so the devices must be turned off within microseconds. In a CSI the link inductor limits di/dt and the rectifier controls I<sub>d</sub>, so a short only stops the power flow. A CSI tolerates it; its dangerous fault is an open circuit.

Regeneration: a CSI returns energy by reversing the link voltage with a phase-controlled rectifier (firing angle above 90°) while I<sub>d</sub> keeps its direction; no extra converter is needed. A diode-fed VSI cannot return energy and needs an active front end or a braking resistor.

Commutation: at 5 MW, a synchronous motor run over-excited supplies the leading current that turns the thyristors off (a load-commutated inverter), so cheap, rugged thyristors can be used. Starting needs pulsed link current until the motor has about a tenth of its speed.

answer.text: Comparison for this duty:

answer: Costs of the CSI: the large choke, a lagging input power factor at low speed, six-step torque ripple that needs attention for torsional resonance, and slower dynamic response.

Harmonics to the motor: the six-step current of an LCI has a 5th of 20 % and a 7th of 14 %, which produce sixth-harmonic torque pulsations; for a pump with a stiff shaft this is acceptable, and twelve-pulse arrangements reduce it further.

Verdict: for a 5 MW pump, where dynamics are slow and ruggedness and regeneration matter most, the CSI (as an LCI with a synchronous motor) is the better choice; for a fast, compact drive a VSI with an active front end would be chosen instead.
